title: Encoding and decoding with generalised linear models
summary: Neuromatch W1D3 re-paced for a week: the generalised linear model as linear predictor plus nonlinearity plus noise model; encoding a retinal ganglion cell's spike train with a Linear-Gaussian model and then a Poisson GLM (the linear–nonlinear–Poisson model), on recorded data the tutorial provides for tutorial purposes; decoding choices from population activity with logistic regression on the Steinmetz data; L2 and L1 regularisation, cross-validated; and the discipline of evaluating against chance, checking for leakage and never reading a decoder as a causal claim.

objectives.description: Write the Poisson GLM log-likelihood, derive its gradient and Hessian, show concavity, and interpret the fitted filter as a multiplicative effect on rate.
Derive logistic regression as a GLM with Bernoulli noise, its cross-entropy loss and gradient, and the effect of L2 and L1 penalties on the fitted weights.
Evaluate a decoder against chance and a baseline on held-out trials, name the leakage and imbalance failure cases, and state why decoding accuracy is not evidence of causation.
Distinguish encoding from decoding, recorded data from synthetic, and what a fitted receptive field is evidence of from what it is not.

preparation.description: W1D3 chapter page: Intro, Tutorials 1–2, Outro, day summary.

W1D3 Tutorial 1, GLMs for Encoding: retinal ganglion cell recordings (Uzzell and Chichilnisky 2004, 'provided for tutorial purposes only'), design matrix of stimulus history, Linear-Gaussian fit, Poisson GLM fitted with scipy.optimize.

W1D3 Tutorial 2, Classifiers and regularizers: logistic regression, decoding choices from the Steinmetz data (276 trials, 691 neurons), cross-validation, L2 and L1 penalties, sparsity, choosing the penalty.

activities.title: Lesson: one framework, three models
activities.instructions: Read the lesson before the notebooks. Write the three GLMs (Linear-Gaussian, Poisson, logistic) as a table in the notebook: linear predictor, nonlinearity, noise model, log-likelihood. Note which datasets in this unit are recorded (both tutorials use recordings) and under what terms.

activities.title: Work through the W1D3 tutorials (Neuromatch notebooks)
activities.instructions: Run Tutorials 1–2 in the Neuromatch book (Colab or Kaggle; code BSD-3). In Tutorial 1 build the design matrix yourself and compare the Linear-Gaussian and Poisson predictions before reading the discussion. In Tutorial 2 record the cross-validated accuracy for each penalty strength and keep the table. The datasets are recordings shared for tutorial use; do not copy them elsewhere.

activities.title: Tutorial: likelihoods, gradients and what regularisation does
activities.instructions: Attempt exercises 1 and 2 before asking for hints. Derive in matrix notation; the interpretation parts are graded as strictly as the algebra.

activities.title: Explain: what a fitted filter is evidence of
activities.instructions: Exercise 3, written without the notes open, then compared with the tutorials' own summaries.

activities.title: Retrieval: the unit's formulas
activities.instructions: From memory: the Poisson GLM log-likelihood and its gradient; the logistic function and the cross-entropy; the L2 and L1 penalised objectives; the definition of chance level for a balanced binary task; the three leakage checks.

exitCheck.description: Exercise 1 accepted: Poisson GLM log-likelihood, gradient Xᵀ(y − λ) and negative semidefinite Hessian derived, concavity concluded, the intercept-only MLE and the multiplicative interpretation given; and exercise 2 accepted with the decoder evaluated against chance and the causal misreading avoided.

commonMisconceptions.claim: A high decoding accuracy shows that the neurons cause the behaviour.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Decoding shows that information about the variable is present in the recorded activity, in a form a linear readout can use. Causation needs intervention; a decoder cannot tell a cause from a correlate or a downstream copy (W3D5 returns to this).

commonMisconceptions.claim: The Linear-Gaussian model is just a less accurate version of the Poisson GLM.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They differ in the noise model and the nonlinearity: the Linear-Gaussian model can predict negative rates and treats counts as continuous with constant variance; the Poisson GLM predicts positive rates with variance equal to the mean. Which is appropriate is a question about the data, not about accuracy.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Regularisation is a trick to improve accuracy.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A penalty is a prior on the weights (Gaussian for L2, Laplace for L1); it trades bias for variance and changes what the fitted weights mean. With 691 neurons and 276 trials some prior is unavoidable; the strength is chosen by cross-validation, never on the test set.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Accuracy on the training trials, or on test trials chosen after looking at them, is the model's performance.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Both leak information. Report held-out accuracy from a split fixed before fitting, with feature selection and penalty choice inside the cross-validation loop, against the majority-class baseline and a label-shuffle control.

checks.name: source-locators
checks.evidence: W1D3 chapter page and Tutorials 1–2 opened 2026-10-30; objectives, section structure, models and data statements recorded: Tutorial 1 fits a temporal receptive field of a retinal ganglion cell with a Linear-Gaussian GLM then a Poisson GLM (P(y_t|x_t,θ) = λ^y e^{−λ}/y!, λ = exp(xᵀθ); log-likelihood yᵀlog λ − 1ᵀλ), data attributed to Uzzell and Chichilnisky 2004 'provided for tutorial purposes only'; Tutorial 2 decodes Steinmetz choices (spikes 276 × 691) with logistic regression σ(θᵀx), L2 and L1 penalised objectives with β/2 Σθ² and β/2 Σ|θ|, cross-validation.

checks.name: mathematical-review
checks.evidence: Content agent re-derived: ℓ(θ) = Σ_t [y_t x_tᵀθ − exp(x_tᵀθ)] + const; ∇ℓ = Xᵀ(y − λ); Hessian −Xᵀ diag(λ) X, negative semidefinite, so ℓ is concave and any stationary point is a global maximum (unique if X has full column rank); intercept-only MLE λ = ȳ, i.e. θ₀ = ln ȳ; a unit increase in x_k multiplies λ by e^{θ_k}. Logistic: log-odds θᵀx; negative log-likelihood Σ[−y ln σ − (1 − y) ln(1 − σ)]; gradient Σ(σ(θᵀx_i) − y_i)x_i; L2 adds βθ to the gradient. 48 correct of 60 balanced held-out trials = 0.80 = 80% against a 50% majority baseline.

checks.name: answer-leakage
checks.evidence: The lesson states the Poisson log-likelihood and the logistic model but leaves the gradient, Hessian, concavity, intercept-only MLE and the cross-entropy gradient to the exercises; its numerical examples (θ_k = 0.3 multiplier; p = 0.88 at log-odds 2) differ from the exercise's confusion-table numbers. Reference reasoning only in instructor/.
